subtype: Lost in a game or puzzle [Actor]
passage:
Sunday
Today I built the whole space station with the building blocks Tarun gave me for my birthday. I started after breakfast and I thought it was maybe ten o'clock, but then Mummy called me for lunch and it was two! I didn't even hear her the first time. The hardest bit was the round window. It kept falling out, and I tried three ways, and the third way worked. When it clicked in I shouted YES and Tarun came running. I wasn't hungry the whole time, which is weird because I'm always hungry. Now my fingers hurt a bit but I feel happy and quiet inside. Tomorrow I want to build the rocket part.
Nilesh

qa.q: What was the hardest part of the space station?
qa.a: The round window. It kept falling out.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel after building all morning, and what shows it?
qa.a: Happy and calm; Nilesh writes about feeling "happy and quiet inside" and shouting YES when the window finally clicked in.

qa.q: What choice helped Nilesh solve the window problem?
qa.a: Trying different ways instead of giving up; the third way worked, which kept the challenge just within reach.

qa.q: What was it like for Mummy when lunch was ready?
qa.a: Mummy had to call twice because Nilesh was so absorbed that the first call went unheard.

grounding: A child is so absorbed in a building set that time and hunger vanish, and the hard part feels just within reach.

subtype: Lost in a game or puzzle [Actor]
passage: After the temple fair in Hatta, Payal came home with a wooden puzzle from the toy stall: fifteen pieces that had to make a bullock cart. She sat on the verandah floor with it while her mother, Vandana, went to milk the buffalo. The wheels were easy. The cart body was not. Payal turned one piece every way, frowned, tried another. The shadows moved across the steps. Vandana called twice that the rotis were ready; Payal didn't hear either time. When the last piece slid in, she clapped once, loudly, and only then noticed her stomach growling and the lamp already lit. "I thought it was still afternoon," she told Vandana, grinning so wide her cheeks hurt.

qa.q: How many pieces did the wooden puzzle have?
qa.a: Fifteen pieces, making a bullock cart.

qa.q: Why did Payal clap loudly when the last piece slid in?
qa.a: She was delighted to solve the hard part after so much turning and trying; the joy of finishing came all at once.

qa.q: What made the puzzle a good fit for Payal's absorption?
qa.a: It had easy parts and a harder part she could just manage with patience, so it kept her working without making her give up.

qa.q: What was it like for Vandana to call twice with no answer?
qa.a: Vandana may have been puzzled or a little annoyed at first, then amused to see her daughter so lost in the puzzle she thought it was still afternoon.

grounding: A child in a small town is so absorbed in a well-matched puzzle that she forgets food and time.

subtype: Lost in a game or puzzle [Actor]
passage: On a rainy Saturday in Melbourne, Tuan dragged out the marble-run set he'd had for a year and never finished. This time he tried the big design on the back of the box, the one with the double spiral. Tomas, his neighbour, came over at ten to play video games. By twelve Tomas was lying on the couch reading a comic, because Tuan hadn't looked up once. The spiral kept jamming. Tuan tilted a piece, tested it with one marble, tilted it again. His grandmother set a bowl of noodles beside him; they went cold. At half past two a marble rolled all the way down, clicked through both spirals and dropped into the cup. Tuan looked at the clock and his mouth fell open. "Where did the day go?"

qa.q: What design did Tuan try from the back of the box?
qa.a: The big design with the double spiral.

qa.q: Why was Tuan so surprised when he looked at the clock?
qa.a: He had been so absorbed in fixing the jams that he hadn't felt the hours pass; it seemed far too soon to be half past two.

qa.q: What choice kept Tuan going when the spiral jammed?
qa.a: Testing with one marble and adjusting a piece at a time, which turned a frustrating jam into small solvable steps.

qa.q: How might Tomas feel about the day?
qa.a: Tomas came to play video games and ended up reading alone on the couch, so Tomas may feel a bit left out, even while impressed when the marble finally runs.

grounding: A child becomes absorbed in a marble-run challenge that matches his skill, forgetting food and time.

passage: Saturday hobby club at the community library ended at one, but at twenty past, Trisha, ten, was still on the floor of the activity room with the gear kit. She was building a windmill whose blades turned when you wound a handle. On the first two tries, the gears slipped. On the third she moved the small gear one peg lower, held her breath and wound. The blades spun. She whooped, then immediately started on a second set of blades. Deepika Ma'am, the volunteer, was stacking chairs. "Trisha, your Papa's outside. And you haven't eaten your tiffin." Trisha looked up, blinking, as if waking. "It's already over?" The tiffin box sat unopened beside her, next to a heap of spare gears.

qa.q: What was Trisha building with the gear kit?
qa.a: A windmill whose blades turned when you wound a handle.

qa.q: What does Trisha's 'It's already over?' suggest about how she felt while building?
qa.a: She was so absorbed that time and hunger vanished 😊; the task was just hard enough to hold all her attention, and that felt joyful.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Trisha's building, and what did she do next?
qa.a: Moving the small gear one peg lower on the third try made the blades spin; instead of stopping, she began a second set, pulled on by a challenge that matched her skill.

qa.q: How might the scene look to Deepika Ma'am, stacking chairs?
qa.a: Deepika Ma'am sees a child so absorbed she missed the end of club and her lunch, and is probably amused and pleased while gently bringing her back to Papa waiting outside.

grounding: A child building with a gear kit loses track of time and food because the challenge matches her skill.

subtype: Lost in a game or puzzle [Actor]
passage: I'm Lakshmi, Sangeeta's older sister. On Sunday morning she tipped out the tub of building bricks and decided to build a bridge between the two beds, long enough for her toy bus to cross. It kept sagging in the middle. She frowned, pulled pieces off, tried a double layer, tried a pillar of stacked bricks underneath. I called her for breakfast twice. Nothing. Amma put a plate of idlis beside her, and she ate one without looking, still clicking bricks with her other hand. I don't know exactly what was going on in her head, but her tongue was poking out and she was humming. At half past twelve the bus rolled across. She sat back, beaming, and said, "Now a tunnel."

qa.q: What did Sangeeta want the bridge to carry?
qa.a: Her toy bus.

qa.q: What do Sangeeta's humming and poking tongue suggest about her state?
qa.a: She seems happily absorbed, challenged but not defeated, so the sagging bridge felt like a puzzle to solve rather than a frustration.

qa.q: What choice did Amma make, and why did it work well?
qa.a: Amma put the idlis beside Sangeeta instead of pulling her away, so she could eat without breaking her concentration on the bridge.

qa.q: How might being ignored at breakfast feel for Lakshmi?
qa.a: Lakshmi might be a little annoyed after calling twice for nothing, but also amused and impressed to see Sangeeta so wrapped up in the bridge 😄

grounding: An older sister watches a child so absorbed in a building-brick bridge that she forgets breakfast and the time.
